Article.ArticleTitle: The Last 25 Years of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Epidemiology-and the Next 25?

Abstract.AbstractText: Considerable new knowledge regarding the epidemiology of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults arose from large-scale population-based epidemiologic investigations that initiated in the late 1980s to 1990s; these investigations have continued to produce relevant findings in recent years. In this Perspective, we briefly comment on the past 25 years of adult population-based OSA epidemiology and discuss selected ways in which the field can further progress over the coming decades. Population-based studies have shown that OSA is common in both men and women, and that prevalence is increasing. OSA is approximately one-third heritable and major predictors of prevalent OSA are obesity, male sex, older age, and interactions among these factors. Severe OSA is consistently associated with a wide range of afflictions-sleepiness, car crashes, depressed mood, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular morbidity, cognitive and metabolic dysfunction, and accelerated mortality-whereas associations of these outcomes with mild-tomoderate OSA have not been as consistently demonstrated. Pressing questions remain regarding the role of years' exposure to less severe OSA in vascular, brain, and heart pathology, cancer risk, and suboptimal functioning in middle-aged to older adults. Because mild-moderate OSA is common and usually untreated, accurately characterizing associations of OSA with these outcomes remains a challenging mandate for the field. Furthermore, research aimed at disentangling the time course of effects of OSA and developing comprehensive methods to characterize varied OSA phenotypes is necessary. Progress will also be made using existing data via consortium collaborations, and interrogations of electronic health records and high-quality data repositories.
